passages.happening:
Jesus calls his twelve disciples to him and gives them authority to drive out unclean spirits and to heal every disease and sickness. This is the work he has been doing himself (9:35). Now he shares it.

Matthew lists their names: first Simon, called Peter, and his brother Andrew; James son of Zebedee and his brother John; Philip and Bartholomew; Thomas and Matthew the tax collector; James son of Alphaeus and Thaddaeus; Simon the Zealot, and Judas Iscariot, “who betrayed Jesus.”
passages.hearers:
Twelve was not a random number. Israel had twelve tribes. By choosing twelve, Jesus was showing that he had come to gather and renew God's people.

The word ‘apostle’ means one who is sent, a messenger with authority to speak for the one who sent him. This is the only place where Matthew uses the word, at the moment they are sent.

The list appears four times in the New Testament (here; Mark 3:16-19; Luke 6:14-16; Acts 1:13). Peter always comes first, and Judas, where he appears, comes last. Matthew alone calls Peter ‘first’ and calls himself ‘the tax collector’. He sets the names in pairs, perhaps because Jesus sent them out two by two (Mark 6:7). Where Matthew and Mark have Thaddaeus, Luke and Acts have ‘Judas son of James’. Most think these are two names for one man.

The group is a strange mix. Matthew had collected taxes for a ruler who served Rome. Simon is called ‘the Zealot’, from a word meaning ‘zealous’. It may mean zeal for God's law, or it may link him with Jews who wanted to resist Rome by force; readers differ. Either way, a tax collector and a zealot were sent out side by side.

‘Iscariot’ is most often explained as ‘man of Kerioth’, a town in the south of Judah (Joshua 15:25). Others link it with a Latin word for a dagger-man, an assassin. John's Gospel calls Judas “the son of Simon Iscariot” (John 6:71), which suggests it was a family name.
passages.hard: Why would Jesus choose Judas, who would betray him? The Gospels do not fully say. They name him as one of the twelve, with the same authority and the same calling as the rest. Matthew does not hide the betrayal; he writes it into the list. The church has always had to live with the fact that one of its first leaders fell, and that being close to Jesus is not the same as belonging to him.
passages.asks: Jesus gave his authority to ordinary men with mixed pasts and opposite opinions, one of whom would betray him. Ask whom you would have left off the list. And ask what it means that he chose to work through people like these, and like you.

passages.t: Sent to the lost sheep of Israel
passages.happening:
Jesus sends the twelve out with instructions. “Do not go onto the road of the Gentiles or enter any town of the Samaritans. Go rather to the lost sheep of Israel.” They are to preach that the kingdom of heaven is near, heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, and drive out demons. “Freely you have received; freely give.”

They are to take no gold, silver or copper, no bag, no second tunic, no sandals, no staff, “for the worker is worthy of his provisions.” In each town they are to find a worthy person and stay with him. Entering a home, they are to greet it. If the home is worthy, their peace will rest on it; if not, it will return to them. Where no one welcomes them, they are to shake the dust off their feet as they leave. It will be more bearable for Sodom and Gomorrah on the day of judgment than for that town.
passages.hearers:
Galilee was ringed by other peoples: the Phoenician cities of Tyre and Sidon to the north-west, the Greek cities of the Decapolis across the lake, and Samaria to the south. The Samaritans worshipped the God of Israel and kept the books of Moses, but they worshipped on their own mountain, Mount Gerizim. Their temple there had been destroyed by the Jewish ruler John Hyrcanus, most likely around 110 BC, and bitterness ran both ways. John's Gospel notes simply, “Jews do not associate with Samaritans” (John 4:9).

Travellers carried coins in a belt, bread in a bag, a spare tunic for cold nights, sandals, and a staff. The twelve are to go without them. The word in verse 9 means ‘acquire’ or ‘get for yourselves’. They are not to equip themselves for the road or make money from their healing. They are to depend on the people who welcome them. Mark's version allows a staff and sandals (Mark 6:8-9), while Matthew and Luke rule out the staff. Some think Mark means the staff a man already has, and Matthew forbids getting another; others think the Gospels apply one teaching in slightly different ways.

Paul later used the saying about the worker being worthy of his pay to defend support for those who preach (1 Corinthians 9:14). An early Christian manual, the Didache, warned that a travelling teacher who stayed three days or asked for money was false. Freely received meant freely given.

The greeting on entering a house was ‘peace’, shalom in Hebrew, a blessing and not just a hello. Shaking the dust off your feet was a public sign of breaking off. Paul and Barnabas did it when a city drove them out (Acts 13:51).
passages.ot:
Sodom and Gomorrah were the Bible's great example of a city judged by God (Genesis 19). To say that judgment will be ‘more bearable’ for them than for a town that refused Jesus' messengers was a shocking thing to say to Jewish hearers. It means that the more light a town is given, the more it will answer for.

‘Lost sheep’ echoes the prophets. Ezekiel spoke of God's people scattered “for lack of a shepherd” (Ezekiel 34:5), and in the previous chapter Jesus looked on the crowds as “sheep without a shepherd” (9:36).
passages.hard:
Why does Jesus tell the twelve not to go to Gentiles or Samaritans, when at the end of the Gospel he sends them to “make disciples of all nations” (28:19)? Is Matthew contradicting itself?

Some critical scholars think so. They suggest that Jesus himself limited his work to Israel, and that the mission to the nations was a later step by the church, read back into the Gospel. Others have been troubled by the limit itself, as if God's kindness stopped at a border.

Most readers see an order, not a contradiction. God made his promises to Israel first, and Jesus begins there. Later Jesus says, “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (15:24), and then helps a Canaanite woman anyway. Paul describes the same order: the gospel is for everyone who believes, “first to the Jew, then to the Greek” (Romans 1:16). And Matthew has already honoured Gentiles, from the women in Jesus' family tree and the wise men from the east to the Roman officer in chapter 8. In this very chapter Jesus says his followers will stand before governors and kings “as witnesses to them and to the Gentiles” (10:18). After his resurrection the doors open to all nations, and ‘all nations’ still includes Israel. The first mission was a first step, not the last word.
passages.asks: Jesus told the twelve to begin close to home, with their own people. Ask who the ‘lost sheep’ nearest to you are. And notice the rule: freely you have received, freely give. Ask what you have been given that you have kept to yourself.

passages.happening:
“Behold, I am sending you out like sheep among wolves; therefore be as shrewd as snakes and as innocent as doves.” Jesus warns the twelve that they will be handed over to local councils and flogged in synagogues, and brought before governors and kings for his sake. When that happens, they are not to worry about what to say: the Spirit of their Father will speak through them.

Families will turn on each other. They will be hated by everyone because of his name, but the one who perseveres to the end will be saved. When persecuted in one town, they are to flee to the next. “Truly I tell you, you will not reach all the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes.” A disciple is not above his teacher. If they have called the head of the house Beelzebul, how much more his household.
passages.hearers:
The warnings fit what happened to the first Christians. ‘Councils’ were local Jewish courts. The Law limited a flogging to forty lashes (Deuteronomy 25:3), and the Mishnah, written down later, sets the number at forty less one, thirty-nine, to be sure the limit was not crossed. Paul says, “Five times I received from the Jews the forty lashes minus one” (2 Corinthians 11:24). Governors and kings had power over life and death. King Herod had James, one of the twelve named in this chapter, “put to death with the sword” (Acts 12:2). Paul later stood before the governors Felix and Festus and King Agrippa (Acts 24 to 26).

‘Hated by everyone because of My name’ matches what Roman writers said. Tacitus wrote that Nero blamed Christians for the great fire of Rome in AD 64 and had many killed. Around AD 111 or 112, Pliny, a Roman governor in what is now northern Turkey, wrote to the emperor Trajan asking whether the name ‘Christian’ by itself should be punished.

The pictures come from the countryside. Wolves were the shepherd's worst enemy. The serpent in Eden was ‘crafty’ (Genesis 3:1), but doves could stand for being easily fooled: Hosea calls Ephraim “a silly, senseless dove” (Hosea 7:11). Jesus wants both qualities at their best: clever without being sly, pure without being naive.

‘Beelzebul’ may mean something like ‘lord of the house’. Jesus calls himself ‘the head of the house’. If his enemies named him after a demon (9:34; 12:24), his followers should not expect better.
passages.ot:
Brother against brother, children against parents, echoes the prophet Micah, who mourned a time when “a daughter rises against her mother” and “A man's enemies are the members of his own household” (Micah 7:6). Jesus will quote Micah directly in verses 35 and 36.

The promise that the Spirit will give them words recalls Moses, who told God he was “slow of speech and tongue” and was told, “I will help you as you speak, and I will teach you what to say” (Exodus 4:10, 12).
passages.hard:
Verse 23 is one of the hardest in Matthew: “you will not reach all the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes.” Did Jesus promise to return before the twelve had finished their mission, and was he wrong?

Some have said yes. Albert Schweitzer built his famous picture of Jesus, published in German in 1906 and in English as The Quest of the Historical Jesus, largely on this chapter. He argued that Jesus expected the end to come while the twelve were still on the road, and that events proved him wrong. Many skeptics take this verse, with 16:28 and 24:34, as an unfulfilled prediction. The objection is serious and deserves a straight answer.

Christians have answered in several ways. John Chrysostom, a preacher of the late 300s, read it as a comfort for frightened messengers: Jesus would come and rejoin them before they had gone through all the towns. Others connect it with Daniel 7, where the Son of Man comes to God to receive power, and read it of Jesus' vindication: at his resurrection, when “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me” (28:18), or in the judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70. Others read it of the final coming, and note that Matthew never says the mission to Israel is finished; on this view the work goes on until he returns. Each reading has careful defenders and real difficulties. When and how Jesus will return is a question on which faithful Christians differ. That he will return is confessed by all.

The verse's purpose in its setting is plain: messengers under pressure are to keep moving, because their Lord's coming will overtake their work.
passages.asks: Jesus did not promise his followers safety. He promised his presence and his words. If you face mockery or loss because you follow him, notice that he tells his messengers to flee danger, not to seek it. And ask how you can be shrewd and gentle at the same time with someone who opposes your faith.

passages.t: Do not be afraid: the sparrows
passages.happening:
Three times Jesus says, ‘Do not be afraid.’ Nothing hidden will stay hidden. What he tells them in the dark, they are to say in the daylight; what is whispered in their ear, they are to shout from the housetops.

“Do not be afraid of those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Instead, fear the One who can destroy both soul and body in hell.” Two sparrows are sold for a penny, yet not one falls to the ground apart from the Father. Even the hairs of your head are all numbered. “So do not be afraid; you are worth more than many sparrows.”

Whoever confesses Jesus before others, he will confess before his Father in heaven. Whoever denies him before others, he will deny before his Father.
passages.hearers:
Houses had flat roofs, and a roof was the natural place to call out news to the street below.

The ‘penny’ was an assarion, a small copper coin worth a tiny part of a day's wage. Sparrows were small, cheap birds sold for food. In Luke's version, five sparrows sell for two pennies (Luke 12:6), as if the fifth were thrown in for nothing. Even that one is not forgotten by God.

The Greek of verse 29 says only that no sparrow falls ‘without your Father’. Many Bibles, the BSB among them, add ‘the will of’ to make the sense clear. Others keep the bare words, which speak of the Father's presence with the sparrow as much as his decision about it.

‘Hell’ here translates Gehenna, the name of the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, where some kings of Judah had burned children in sacrifice to false gods (Jeremiah 7:31). By Jesus' day the name stood for the place of final judgment. The idea that it was a burning rubbish dump appears only many centuries later and has no ancient support.
passages.ot:
‘Not a hair of his head will fall to the ground’ was an old way of promising someone's safety (1 Samuel 14:45). Jesus goes further: the hairs are not just kept but counted.

‘Fear the LORD’ runs through the whole Old Testament. It means the deep reverence that puts God first, and it is called “the beginning of wisdom” (Proverbs 9:10). Jesus sets the right fear against the wrong one. Fear God, and you need not fear anyone else.
passages.hard:
Who is ‘the One who can destroy both soul and body in hell’? Most readers take it to be God, the only judge with that power. A few have suggested the devil, but Scripture never gives the devil authority over hell, and the next verse turns straight to the Father's care.

What is hell like? Christians agree that Jesus warned of real and final judgment. They differ on its nature. The view most widely held through church history is that it is endless, conscious separation from God. Others hold that the wicked will finally cease to exist, and they point to this very verse, where God can ‘destroy’ soul and body. Still others hope that God's love will in the end restore all people. These notes state the views and do not settle the question.

The warning is not meant to frighten anyone into faith, and it is not meant to sit alone. Jesus says ‘Do not be afraid’ three times in these few verses. The God who could destroy is the Father who counts the hairs on your head and notices a sparrow fall. If you are afraid of God's judgment, hear the same voice that says, “Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest” (11:28).

And ‘whoever denies Me’? Peter denied Jesus three times on the night of his arrest (26:69-75), and Jesus restored him afterwards (John 21:15-19). The warning is about a settled turning away, not about a frightened failure that is wept over and forgiven.
passages.asks: Name something you are afraid of right now. Then put it beside the sparrow: sold for almost nothing, and not one falls without your Father. You are worth more than many sparrows. If you are grieving someone, he knew the hour they fell, and he was not absent.

passages.happening:
“Do not assume that I have come to bring peace to the earth; I have not come to bring peace, but a sword.” Jesus has come to turn a man against his father, a daughter against her mother, a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law. A man's enemies will be the members of his own household.

Anyone who loves father or mother, son or daughter, more than him is not worthy of him. Anyone who does not take up his cross and follow him is not worthy of him. “Whoever finds his life will lose it, and whoever loses his life for My sake will find it.”
passages.hearers:
In Jesus' world the family was everything: your work, your home, your worship, your good name, and your safety in old age. A son or daughter-in-law who broke with the family over Jesus could lose all of that. Many early believers did.

The cross meant only one thing to first-century hearers. It was Rome's way of executing slaves and rebels, and the condemned man carried the crossbeam to his own death. To ‘take up his cross’ was not a picture of a small daily trouble. It meant being ready to lose everything, even life. This is the first time Matthew mentions the cross, long before Jesus carries his own.

Luke gives a sharper form of the saying about family: anyone who does not ‘hate’ father and mother cannot be Jesus' disciple (Luke 14:26). In the Hebrew way of speaking, ‘hate’ can mean ‘love less’ when two loves are compared. Genesis says Jacob “loved Rachel more than Leah”, and the next verse, in Hebrew, says Leah was ‘hated’, which the BSB rightly translates as “unloved” (Genesis 29:30-31). Matthew's wording says the same thing plainly: love Jesus more. Some readers think the word ‘hate’ was chosen because a comparison alone is too gentle; either way, the point is first place.
passages.ot:
Verses 35 and 36 quote Micah 7:6, where the prophet grieves over a society so broken that “a son dishonors his father” and “A man's enemies are the members of his own household.” Jesus does not say that this breakdown is good. He says that his coming will bring that kind of division as a result, because people will answer him differently, even within one home.

Isaiah had called the coming king “Prince of Peace” (Isaiah 9:6). The peace Jesus brings is real, but it is not the peace of everyone agreeing to leave him out.
passages.hard:
‘Not peace, but a sword’ is a picture of division, not a call to violence. Jesus is describing what his coming will do: it will split people, even families, as some follow him and some do not. He never told his followers to fight for him. When Peter drew a sword to defend him, Jesus said, “Put your sword back in its place” and “all who draw the sword will die by the sword” (26:52). The same Jesus said, “Blessed are the peacemakers” (5:9). No one may use this verse to justify harming anyone, inside a family or outside it.

Nor is it a command to cut off your family. Jesus condemned those who neglected their parents (15:4-6). Paul tells believers, “If it is possible on your part, live at peace with everyone” (Romans 12:18), and Peter says to give the reason for your hope “with gentleness and respect” (1 Peter 3:15). The division Jesus speaks of comes from others' response to him, not from his followers' hostility.

If your family has rejected you for your faith, you are not alone, and you have not failed. The psalmist wrote, “Though my father and mother forsake me, the LORD will receive me” (Psalm 27:10). Jesus promised that no one who has left home or family for his sake will lose out (Mark 10:29-30). Keep loving them, keep the door open as far as you safely can, and find a church family who will stand with you. If rejection has turned into threats or harm, seeking safety is not disloyalty to Jesus. Please speak to someone you trust, and if you are in danger, contact the police or a crisis line.
passages.asks: Jesus asks for first place, above even the people you love most. That is not a call to love them less than you do now. It is a call to love him more. Ask honestly whom you would choose if the two loves pulled apart. And ask what ‘losing your life’ for him might look like this week, in small things.

passages.happening: Jesus ends his instructions with a promise. Whoever receives his messengers receives him, and whoever receives him receives the One who sent him. Whoever receives a prophet because he is a prophet will receive a prophet's reward, and whoever receives a righteous person will receive a righteous person's reward. “And if anyone gives even a cup of cold water to one of these little ones because he is My disciple, truly I tell you, he will never lose his reward.”
passages.hearers:
In the ancient world, a messenger stood for the one who sent him. To welcome the messenger was to welcome the sender, and to insult the messenger was to insult the sender. Jesus applies this to his followers: welcome them, and you welcome him, and through him, God.

A cup of cold water was the smallest kindness one could offer in a hot, dry land. Anyone could give it.

‘Little ones’ in Matthew means Jesus' disciples, not only children. Later he warns against causing “one of these little ones who believe in Me” to stumble (18:6). The phrase reminds the twelve that, for all their authority, they will often be weak and in need.
passages.hard: Does this mean we earn reward from God by our kindness? Christians have long read Jesus' talk of reward as the Father's generous delight in what his children do, not as wages that buy salvation. The reward is promised for a cup of water, which is to say for almost nothing. That is how generous God is. In chapter 25 those who fed and welcomed ‘the least of these’ are surprised to learn that they did it for Jesus (25:40).
passages.asks: The chapter that began with authority over demons ends with a cup of water. Some are sent; others welcome those who are sent, and both matter to Jesus. Ask who in your life is carrying the message and could use a welcome, a meal, a bed, or a cup of water. That small thing is not lost.
